title: Rafale Marine Lands on INS Vikrant on First Attempt in Carrier Trials
excerpt: The October 29 arrested landing is the first step toward operationalising India's 26-jet, Rs 63,000 crore Rafale Marine purchase on its ski-jump carriers.
body:
• A Rafale Marine jet landed on INS Vikrant on its maiden attempt on October 29, the Indian Navy confirmed on October 30.
  • The trials are the first steps toward operationalising the aircraft, after shore-based tests at INS Hansa in Goa.
  • India signed an agreement with France on April 28, 2025, for 26 Rafale Marine jets worth about Rs 63,000 crore — 22 single-seat and four twin-seat.
  • Deliveries are expected to begin in late 2028 or 2029 and conclude by 2030-31; the jets will operate from INS Vikrant and INS Vikramaditya.

A Rafale Marine fighter aircraft successfully carried out an arrested landing on the Indian Navy's indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant on October 29, completing the manoeuvre on its maiden attempt. The Indian Navy confirmed the milestone on October 30.

"A Rafale Marine aircraft successfully landed onboard Indian Navy's indigenous Aircraft Carrier INS Vikrant on its maiden attempt on 29 Oct 26. The ongoing trials mark the first steps towards operationalisation of the aircraft in the Indian Navy," the Navy said, according to SSB Crack. The landing was conducted under the command of Captain Ashok Rao, commanding officer of INS Vikrant, and the Navy released video footage. India Sentinels also reported the first-attempt landing on Thursday.

From shore trials to the deck

The carrier landing followed shore-based trials at the Shore-Based Test Facility at INS Hansa in Goa. That facility replicates the ski-jump ramp and arrestor-wire systems used by Indian carriers and was used to assess the modifications required for the Rafale M to operate from INS Vikrant.

Carrier trials of this kind check how an aircraft behaves on approach to the deck, in ski-jump launch, in arrested recovery and in handling on the flight deck, as well as how it works with the ship's arresting gear, India Sentinels noted. The Rafale M has a reinforced undercarriage and a tailhook for such landings.

A technical mismatch the trials must prove out

The Rafale M was designed for Catapult Assisted Take-Off But Arrested Recovery (CATOBAR) operations, as used on the French Navy's carrier Charles de Gaulle. INS Vikrant uses Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery (STOBAR): aircraft take off from a ski-jump ramp and are recovered using arrestor wires. The successful maiden landing validates the aircraft's compatibility with the STOBAR system after the necessary assessments, SSB Crack reported.

One practical constraint remains the jet's fixed, non-folding wings, with a span of about 10.9 metres — wider than Vikrant's aircraft lifts at roughly 10 metres, which were designed for the folding-wing MiG-29K. Work is under way to modify the lifts, and procedures may include temporarily removing wingtip pylons during transfers between flight deck and hangar. Similar constraints exist on INS Vikramaditya.

The Rs 63,000 crore acquisition behind it

India and France signed an intergovernmental agreement on April 28, 2025, for 26 Rafale Marine aircraft valued at approximately Rs 63,000 crore. The package comprises 22 single-seat fighters and four twin-seat trainers, along with weapons, simulators, training and logistics support.

The twin-engine Rafale M, built by Dassault Aviation, can carry out air defence, maritime strike, reconnaissance and deep-strike missions, with weapons including Meteor beyond-visual-range missiles, MICA missiles, SCALP cruise missiles and Exocet anti-ship missiles. Once inducted, it will operate alongside and eventually help replace the Navy's MiG-29K fleet, serving as an interim capability until the indigenous Twin-Engine Deck-Based Fighter becomes available. Commonality with the Indian Air Force's 36 Rafales should ease logistics and spares support.

INS Vikrant, built by Cochin Shipyard and commissioned on September 2, 2022, displaces about 45,000 tonnes. A MiG-29K and the naval variant of the Light Combat Aircraft made its first fixed-wing landings on February 6, 2023; the Rafale M is now the third fixed-wing type to land on the ship.

What happens next

Further trials will continue to establish the aircraft's full operational suitability for sustained carrier operations. Deliveries of India's own aircraft are expected to begin from late 2028 or 2029 and conclude by 2030-31, operating from both INS Vikrant and INS Vikramaditya. Until then, the MiG-29K remains the carriers' embarked fighter.
